author: @goodside
text:
I feel like we need a unified theory of what LLMs can’t do.

Most issues (calculation, string ops, grounding) can be patched (via tools, retrieval) so we see them as trivial, not as omens of subtler but similarly fundamental limits. But why is this true?
summary: Calls for a unified theory of what LLMs cannot do, noting that patching failures with tools and retrieval may hide subtler fundamental limits.

notable_replies.author: @goodside
notable_replies.text: Feels suspiciously lucky we can just bolt on plugins for things we *know* the model will never do and we’re done — that all problems will yield to scale except these few.

notable_replies.author: @mayfer
notable_replies.text:
i have an idea that i suck at putting into words but let me try

true understanding requires a fully geometric grasp that includes invariants & constraints the same way 3d rotation preserves the object's shape

formal reasoning requires a mapping of n-dimensional representations with invariants analogous to the problem space

LLMs' single-forward-pass architecture means that all of the geometry of the problem space has to fit in one forward pass (bc even the 1 next token is crucial to producing a correct output) so it ends up failing to represent any problem that doesn't fit into one lightning strike from input to output

a properly recurrent algorithm that does diffusion on the internal representation w/ changing input, even before outputting a single token, is likely going to be able to include many more invariants & geometric constraints, because they will have the chance to settle into the time domain

notable_replies.author: @sytelus
notable_replies.text:
Why such a limited set of evals? If these models are meant for research, extensive evals at different checkpoints are all the more important. They are not even that hard to run :). On the other hand, too many papers tend to omit evals where model is not doing well which wouldn’t be good science.

IMO, we need to stop comparing with OPT and BLOOM. OPT is massively undertrained and had huge issues in training itself. If model is matching OPT level perf, it’s probably an issue. Same for BLOOM as it is also noted in this paper that multilingual data is of much lower quality.

One thing I keep suspecting is that there is some issue with Pile, especially how Common Crawl was filtered. Models trained on Pile generally seem to leg behind significantly for similar number of tokens from private datasets held at OpenAI/Fair (ex, recent LLaMA carefully avoided most of the Pile).

linked_content.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale? To answer these questions, we introduce \textit{Pythia}, a suite of 16 LLMs all trained on public data seen in the exact same order and ranging in size from 70M to 12B parameters. We provide public access to 154 checkpoints for each one of the 16 models, alongside tools to download and reconstruct their exact training dataloaders for further study. We intend \textit{Pythia} to facilitate research in many areas, and we present several case studies including novel results in memorization, term frequency effects on few-shot performance, and reducing gender bias. author: @RSS_D4
text:
The timing of @elonmusk  data scraping rules and @OpenAI widening the release of "browsing" function are not coincidence. Pretty much all content/IP is going to need to move behind paywalls, to blockchain or something similar to charge microtransactions for interactions/pageviews. 

I don't understand how ad based internet business models are going to work if you create content and then it's gobbled up by an LLM once and then shown to 1000s of people who might ask a similar question. Are advertisers paying when ChatGPT says "clicking on link"?

I've seen this specifically with travel related questions where LLMs will essentially spit out verbatim the suggestions of a travel blog. This is different from Google search because for the most part you still need to click on the link with Google to get answers and then served with ads.
summary: Argues that LLMs answering from scraped content break ad-funded web business models, predicting content will move behind paywalls or blockchain micropayments, citing verbatim travel-blog answers.

notable_replies.text:
Again, LLMs not meant to be used for search, but basic question answer will be gone.

That said, I expect much of the internet to go closed garden with the abuse many AI providers are using to extract info.

That said, for things that require live updates LLMs won’t be it. 

The future may be paying to bias an AI towards your product similar to google auditioning top placement

author: @_jasonwei
text:
For any new prompting technique (e.g., tree-of-thought, least-to-most, graph-of-thoughts prompting), I consider four things to decide if it will become widely adopted:

1. How easy is it to implement
2. How much compute it use
3. How many tasks does it improve
4. How much does it improve those tasks

Here is my read of a few techniques:

Chain-of-thought prompting is a strong baseline because it improves many reasoning tasks by a large margin. It uses more compute than giving the answer immediately but is easy to implement (“let’s think step-by-step”, only a single pass through the LLM).

Majority vote / consensus / self-consistency is also a nice baseline, with trivial implementation and large improvements on many tasks. However, it costs much more compute than a single chain-of-thought.

Least-to-most / plan-and-solve / decomposition prompting takes some time to implement (requires multiple passes, some error catching), requires significant prompt engineering, and uses a lot of compute. This is a decent amount of friction. However, it may improve very complicated tasks a lot if you have a capable-enough language model.

Tree-of-thought / graph-of-thought prompting / cascades is a pretty elegant approach IMHO but it requires substantial overhead to implement, since you make multiple calls to a language model and you have to program them and potentially backtrack in some non-trivial way. So this is not really worth doing unless the performance gain will be very large. My guess is that right now it may be hard to find tasks worth doing this for, but as we train better language models and ask them to do more-complicated tasks this will gain more traction.

Forcing the reasoning to be entirely in code (program-of-thoughts, scratchpad) is also a really nice idea, especially since GPT-4 is so good at programming and reasoning ability seems stronger when it’s coupled with code. Obviously the point of this is to have the infra to actually execute the code, but even if you don’t have the infra for that, it could be a strong baseline to ask the language model to predict the output of executing the code (perhaps step-by-step).
summary: Proposes four criteria for whether a prompting technique gets adopted (ease, compute, breadth, size of gains) and assesses chain-of-thought, self-consistency, decomposition, tree-of-thought and code-based reasoning.

author: @pwang
text:
As multiple crises pop off, we might be finally crossing the threshold into liminality.

This is not a good thing!
This is not some hippie Age-of-Aquarius bullshit.

Liminality means people are on their own when it comes to sense-making. COVID was our “gear check” as a species and we failed horribly.

Liminal zones for individuals is when new internal subjective states can be accessed, because you *have to* depart old ones. You *cannot* stay the same. It’s sink-or-swim.

Liminal zones for societies are when revolutions happen. Old ways of sensing and cohering collective truth evaporate, and new cults of awareness appear, and then fight for dominance. Yes, fight. All war is culture war; in a liminal zone, it falls back to an even earlier state: religious war.

It is quite likely that our *only* hope through this is to build an LLM/AI/AGI to facilitate collective sense-making which out-coheres the accelerating pace of liminal events which split us further into microtribes of confusion and delusion.

We don’t need more podcasters “questioning the MSM narrative”. The narrative is crumbling all on its own. But we absolutely don’t want nuclear-capable states with no central narrative.

Every society is like a school of disparate fish, eating each other but swimming together. Moloch is the stigmergy of the school itself.

Boulders of change are now raining down into the ocean of our collective objective reality, and Moloch evaporates as all the fishes and dolphins and whales scramble to form new schools.

The Israel-Hamas conflict will be a source of many boulders of confusion. Next year’s election will be a storm.

My thesis is: whoever or whatever culture can most quickly leverage AI tech and a comms platform like Twitter, Bluesky, or Mastodon to support a *coherent* polyphony of subcultures of sense making, will become the operating system of a new humanity. The defining characteristic will be that it *relies* on AI to exist, just our current industrial world relies of electricity and literacy in order to exist. I think this should be the near-term focus of the e/acc movement.

Who is actually *actually* working on this right now? (Not just gesturing vaguely about it while high at a burn) What projects and resources can we harness? @jim_rutt & @jgreenhall is it time for “rally point gamma”? 😉

But just because it failed at its (stated) mission, and that mission is somewhat aligned with what I'm saying, I don't think it constitutes some ironclad proof of impossibility.

In fact, I think that most historical approaches of trying to "use AI" to solve collective coordination tend to view it as just a smart database or calculator, on theoutside of the throes of human activity which it's trying to calculate.

I've never seen one whose architecture fundamentally centers on human agents weaving the AI-intermediate intersubjectivity into their own sense of self, which is what I'm suggesting.

LLMs represent words as vector embeddings. Do they represent *functions* as vectors too?

Yes! This has implications for how we think about “reasoning” in language models. New preprint w/ @millicent_li, @arnab_api, @amuuueller, @byron_c_wallace, @davidbau:
https://t.co/NCsbctXpMq https://t.co/4hPXlPWtBn
summary: Announces a preprint (Todd et al., Bau lab) showing LLMs encode tasks or functions as vectors, with implications for how 'reasoning' in language models is understood.

notable_replies.author: @ericwtodd
notable_replies.text: LLMs perform a wide array of functions (input-output mapping operations), including NLP tasks. If they contain a vector space for functions, it would allow us to begin decomposing what a function *is* in an LLM. We investigate functions in in-context learning (ICL) prompts. https://t.co/VAiy0cfULw

notable_replies.author: @ericwtodd
notable_replies.text:
How do we localize a function in LLMs?

Given ICL prompts, we use causal mediation analysis and find a few attention heads that encode a task representation. We call this a "function vector" (FV). Interestingly, FVs trigger the execution of specific tasks in zero-shot contexts! https://t.co/vza1401cIt

author: @_akhaliq
text:
Trusted Source Alignment in Large Language Models

paper page: https://t.co/edz1YC86FU

Large language models (LLMs) are trained on web-scale corpora that inevitably include contradictory factual information from sources of varying reliability. In this paper, we propose measuring an LLM property called trusted source alignment (TSA): the model's propensity to align with content produced by trusted publishers in the face of uncertainty or controversy. We present FactCheckQA, a TSA evaluation dataset based on a corpus of fact checking articles. We describe a simple protocol for evaluating TSA and offer a detailed analysis of design considerations including response extraction, claim contextualization, and bias in prompt formulation. Applying the protocol to PaLM-2, we find that as we scale up the model size, the model performance on FactCheckQA improves from near-random to up to 80% balanced accuracy in aligning with trusted sources.
summary: Shares a paper proposing 'trusted source alignment' and the FactCheckQA dataset; on PaLM-2, agreement with trusted sources rises with scale to about 80% balanced accuracy.

notable_replies.author: @jd_pressman
notable_replies.text:
The last time I thought about this my proposed algorithm was:

- Shard your dataset into clustered subsets with high divergence/noncorrelated features when you train

- Initialize the pretrained model with random weights

- Put out a IPFS link (pointed to by a DNS entry/HTTP server) for the weights, the shards, the working groups, and shard assigned to each group

- Each client downloads the weights and their assigned shard of the dataset

- The clients train on the weights for n steps 

(Simplification: Assume that there is a deadline to submit the weights by, and your computer just needs to be fast enough to do those steps and submit by that time. If your computer is faster you can do more steps. Later you'll be verifying identities and duplicating the computations to prevent malicious submissions so the step size will be fixed. You'll also cluster together nodes of similar speed so they can work together.)

- Once ready, clients submit to the C&C server a ready status along with the IPFS hash of their checkpoint

- Each client in a working group downloads each others checkpoints with the list from C&C

- The working groups mutually zipit each others checkpoints and submit the shared hash to C&C

- (Optional depending on the hierarchy of the network), Have the assigned boxes for it compute the next layer(s) of the zipit from the mutual checkpoints 

- Command and Control server takes the last handful of checkpoints and zipits them together

- Server puts out a IPFS link for the new combined weights

notable_replies.author: @jd_pressman
notable_replies.text:
@gfodor You need to be able to train on different distributions of data to get a real speedup from distributed training. Otherwise you just get the same gradient updates in roughly the same order and adding more nodes only decreases variance.

notable_replies.author: @MichaelTontchev
notable_replies.text:
>Black box methods are sufficient for human alignment

This is a misunderstanding of why humans generally behave well in society. It's not that their preferences are tuned to getting along - it's that their cost/benefit analysis concludes that bad actions would be punished due to power that others hold. Give humans total power over their surroundings, and their actions change. (Not to say humans are all selfish/bad, of course, but society isn't nice purely because humans are aligned - it's because actions that make people more powerful with high certainty are rare)

author: @Junger0x
text:
SGX: A possible solution for multi-proofs

TL;DR Cryptographic implementations are complex and not yet mature. To minimize potential errors and vulnerabilities, we need diversity in proof systems. SGX proof can benefit us in this context. Let’s dive in!

Relying on specific elements within blockchain is a departure from the core philosophy of decentralized systems. The preference in such systems is to minimize trust in individuals, machines, or clients, highlighting decentralization as a key factor. This emphasis has been crucial for ensuring system resilience against hacks, malfunctions, or dishonest actions of these parties. However, this ideal of decentralization encounters practical challenges when confronted with the realities of software development.

Allcode, inherently, harbors some vulnerabilities; no system is immune to bugs or resistant to all attack vectors. This is particularly true for complex constructs like ZK circuits, which consist of extensive and intricate codebases. For instance, as Vitalik pointed out, '34,469 lines of code in PSE circuits are not going to be bug-free for a long time.' This acknowledgment of potential flaws necessitates the development of a multi-proof system for ZK-Rollups. Such a system might take various forms: different implementations by different teams, a combination of validity proofs and fraud proofs, or a blend of different types of validity proofs, like ZK and SGX proofs.

As a solution: SGX

SGX refers to Software Guard Extensions, a set of security-related instruction codes built into some Intel CPUs. Its purpose is to protect selected code (it will be proof generation client in rollup context) and data from disclosure or modification by running the code and storing the data in a protected memory area called an enclave.

SGX's main purpose is to enhance the security of application code and data, safeguarding them from malicious software attacks that may be running at higher privilege levels. This is especially crucial in cloud computing environments, where it can be utilized to establish secure execution environments for sensitive applications, even on a potentially compromised host. This secure enclave is minimizing attack vectors.

To briefly summarize the work mechanism;

- Enclave Creation: SGX allows applications to create protected enclaves in memory, where data and code are encrypted and isolated from the rest of the system.
- Secure Processing: Sensitive data is processed inside these enclaves, ensuring its confidentiality and integrity, even from higher-privileged processes and the operating system.
- Remote Attestation: SGX provides a way to verify that software is securely running within an enclave, building trust with external entities.
- Memory Encryption: Data entering and leaving the enclave is encrypted in real-time by the CPU, safeguarding it against unauthorized access.
- Data Sealing: SGX enables data to be encrypted (sealed) for secure storage outside the enclave, accessible only by the enclave it was sealed by.

Blockchain usage

SGX currently has a limited use case on the blockchain. It is used for private smart contracts and by Flashbots for block building. However, we can extend this concept to rollups to construct multi-proofs system.

To advance the on-chain ZK-Rollup state root, we need two state transition proofs; a cryptographic proof (SNARKs) and an SGX proof. A cryptographic proof is a traditional method for ZK-Rollups, but we need to clarify SGX proof here. SGX proofs are generated in two steps:

1) One-time registration: An SGX program first generates an Ethereum (pubkey, privkey) pair. This keypair is tied to a specific SGX enclave, and only signs valid state transitions (pre_state_root, post_state_root, block_root). The pubkey is registered on-chain by verifying an SGX remote attestation which attests to the pubkey being correctly generated.

2) Proving: After registration the SGX program runs the rollup state transition function to sign messages of the form (pre_state_root, post_state_root, block_root). These SGX proofs are verified on-chain by checking signatures against the registered pubkey.

SGX will run the same code as that would be run on a zkVM, which is a light execution client. So instead of a normal client like Geth which needs access to all the chain state to be able to execute transactions, we want proving systems to require only the data that is actually necessary for verifying blocks, only the data is actually needed, and we then verify the correctness of that data as well next to to the execution of the transactions.

The necessary data is signed using a standard ECDSA signature within SGX, utilizing a private key exclusive to SGX. The signature is thenverified in the smart contract.

There are several reasons to use SGX as a different type of proof;

Simplicity: SGX has a much simpler structure than SNARKs. We don't need to make almost any changes to run an existing client.

Latency: Producing SGX proofs is faster than producing SNARKs. There is no additional proof latency.

Liveness: SGX proof doesn't impact liveness.

Drawbacks of SGX

Trust: This approach relies on trusting the SGX technology and its implementation by Intel. Any vulnerabilities in SGX could potentially impact the security of the proof process.

Novelty: It’s use on blockchain is limited and examples are few.

Security: This secure enclave is not self-sufficient. It needs to be combined with ZK, MPC etc.

We can't build a proof system that relies solely on the SGX. Because a potential vulnerability in the enclave means that an attacker who sabotages the proof can mint unlimited coins on the network. Perhaps, as we mentioned at the beginning, it would be ethically problematic to "trust" Intel to make this work. But we use SGX here just for diversity; SNARKs + SGX is a more safety way over just SNARKs.

Conclusion

The systems we build have significant monetary value, making them an attractive target for malicious attackers. However, these systems can be breached not only by malicious attackers but also spontaneously. Therefore, it is necessary to open new defense fronts to avoid such possibilities.

Diversifying our proof methods is one such option. While ZK proofs are already frequently used on ZK-Rollups, we can further diversify our proofs by incorporating SGX proofs. If we can run our light execution client on secure enclave of SGX, we can generate another validity proof to verify rollup blocks. We can easily achieve this by running the existing client we use for proofing on SGX with almost no changes.
summary: Long post proposing Intel SGX enclave proofs alongside SNARKs as a multi-proof system for ZK-rollups to reduce reliance on bug-prone cryptographic circuits; not about AI.

author: @sebkrier
text:
Lasty study tweet for today - a very good socio-technical review of machines as moral agents, patients and proxies. Two things that struck me:

There is a well-established 'machine penalty' in human-machine interactions, in that humans are more likely to cooperate with other humans than they would with a machine. This is understandable in some settings, but frequent cooperation can lead to better results. One potential fix is giving machines human-like traits - but for this to be effective, the machine would have to be deceptively human-like, and anthropomorphism can be risky or problematic. I'm not sure what the right middle-ground is, but a parallel option is to develop new moral norms. This is hard to foster in practice though. Fwiw I'll continue being polite with AI chatbots haha.

Another point I liked also is that humans outsourcing tasks to agents can create psychological factors that facilitate unethical behaviours (anonymity, distance to victims etc) - a bit like how people are more rude to others online or on the road. However with agents, depending on how and where they operate, the scope of harm can be much wider. This makes me think that there should be strong liability linking principals (users) to their agents for serious harms caused; by only considering developers or deployers, you create moral hazards. Looking forward to more papers looking at the many facets to agency and liability! https://t.co/IhAI6d7D3T
summary: Highlights a review of machines as moral agents, patients and proxies, noting the human 'machine penalty' in cooperation, and argues users should bear strong liability for serious harms caused by their agents.

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(1/5) A few years ago, it was widely believed that the first deployment of self-driving would be long-haul trucks on highways, which is a much easier technical problem than city driving.

VCs invested billions based on this theory.

Why did so many people call this wrong?

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(3/5) What actually worked for getting self-driving live was the Cruise / Waymo approach of deploying it in the lowest-risk setting possible.  

The first Cruise cars in SF were only allowed to drive in the middle of the night, in the emptiest part of the city, below 30mph.

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(4/5) I knew self-driving had finally arrived when Cruise cars had been driving themselves for a few weeks with no major mishaps. 

After that, usage expanded basically in order of risk - first to more parts of the city, then more times of the day. Next up is highway driving.

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(5/5) A lot of learnings here for AI startups.  Many startups are working on an AI system that effectively replaces a human doing some important job. 

The best way to get these systems live is to find a way to start with a near zero-risk setting.

linked_content.abstract: To understand the risks posed by a new AI system, we must understand what it can and cannot do. Building on prior work, we introduce a programme of new "dangerous capability" evaluations and pilot them on Gemini 1.0 models. Our evaluations cover four areas: (1) persuasion and deception; (2) cyber-security; (3) self-proliferation; and (4) self-reasoning. We do not find evidence of strong dangerous capabilities in the models we evaluated, but we flag early warning signs. Our goal is to help advance a rigorous science of dangerous capability evaluation, in preparation for future models.

author: @OwainEvans_UK
text:
You'd like to sell some information. If you could show prospective buyers the info, they'd realize it's valuable. But at that point they wouldn't payfor it!
Enter LLMs. LLMs can assess the information, pay for it if it's good, and completely forget it if not. https://t.co/wtDHvFCqPe
summary: Explains the information-selling paradox, where buyers can't value information without seeing it, and proposes LLMs that inspect it, pay if it is good, and forget it otherwise.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
I haven't read the whole paper and so I might have missed this. 
My concern is that the LLM can be adversarial attacked by the information seller. This could convince the LLM to pay for information which is slightly below a quality threshold. (If the information was way below the threshold, then the human principal of the LLM would be more likely to find out.)
This problem would be avoided if the sellers are trusted by the human principal to not use jailbreaks (while the principal is still uncertain about the quality of information).

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text: Paper link: https://t.co/0tl4YkkD1q

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
On the issue of adversarial robustness:
1. If the human is always going to check the purchased information themselves (and they can judge quality), then it should be fine. 
2. If the LLM is acting more autonomously (e.g. making decisions based on purchases), or if the LLM can judge quality better than the human, then there seems to me a problem. 
3. The seller has to also trust that the LLM system doesn't steal the info, either by using a trusted 3rd party for the LLM or by transparency of the code.

text: At some point people will gradually realise the full extent of AI's potential as opposed to seeing it merely as a chatbot. When you're able to start triangulating information about people and inferring (true) things about them, lots of people will be made more vulnerable: doxxing, finding out alts, unearthing private beliefs, highliting inconsistencies, mapping relationships etc. Then people will either further retreat in private spaces and communities, or they will gradually learn to embrace the complexity and necessity of true diversity.

author: @ylecun
text:
It seems to me that before "urgently figuring out how to control AI systems much smarter than us" we need to have the beginning of a hint of a design for a system smarter than a house cat.

Such a sense of urgency reveals an extremely distorted view of reality.
No wonder the more based members of the organization seeked to marginalize the superalignment group.

It's as if someone had said in 1925 "we urgently need to figure out how to control aircrafts that can transport hundreds of passengers at near the speed of the sound over the oceans."
It would have been difficult to make long-haul passenger jets safe before the turbojet was invented and before any aircraft had crossed the atlantic non-stop.
Yet, we can now fly halfway around the world on twin-engine jets in complete safety. 
It didn't require some sort of magical recipe for safety.
It took decades of careful engineering and iterative refinements.

The process will be similar for intelligent systems.
It will take years for them to get as smart as cats, and more years to get as smart as humans, let alone smarter (don't confuse the superhuman knowledge accumulation and retrieval abilities of current LLMs with actual intelligence).
It will take years for them to be deployed and fine-tuned for efficiency and safety as they are made smarter and smarter.
summary: Replying to Jan Leike's exit, argues urgency about controlling superhuman AI is distorted when no design exists for AI smarter than a cat, and that safety will come from iterative engineering, as with jets.

quoted_tweet.text: Stepping away from this job has been one of the hardest things I have ever done, because we urgently need to figure out how to steer and control AI systems much smarter than us.

author: @sebkrier
text:
If we were to actually drastically improve public institutions and institutional decision making, we could probably also tolerate riskier and more innovative policymaking. If you care about AGI risk, you should definitely want to prioritize a competent state. Unfortunately this doesn't mean throwing money at the public sector, but deep structural reform like:

1. Complete HR overhaul including more flexibility in hiring/firing, more consistent performance measurement, and accountability for underperformance. Internal career progression paths that depend on observable metrics and not on hopping around departments. Incentivising more specialization and fewer generalists. Encourage the development of a "portfolio" model for policy advisers like you'd have for academics, reward people for having been a part of well designed policy with measurable outcomes. Don't anonymize experience and successes in HR CV reviews.

2. Addressing the lack of accountability and transparency in decision-making processes within the bureaucracy. This problem is exacerbated by the diffusion of responsibility among various levels of civil servants, making it difficult to identify who has the ultimate authority to make critical decisions. If something doesn't work it should be very quick to pinpoint where the decision originated from.

3. Not blindly delegating policy design to a few private sector stakeholders and thinking this is taking a market friendly approach. When people look at something that benefits a narrow set of stakeholders, they rarely conceive of aggregate effects. They can be advisors though, to help policymakers understand how they operate.

4. Salaries that match the private sector, as Singapore does. This necessarily also means a smaller public sector in some places, and making this career path more prestigious. People should actively strive to go work for the public sector, and not simply because of work-life balance.

5. Mechanisms to continuously review laws and regulations, with an active duty to review them and either improve or undo them. Sunset or periodic review clauses by default for some types of regulations. Incentives to reduce unnecessary paperwork and red tape. See one-in, one-out (or two-out) rules or stuff like 'regulatory guillotines'. I think the Paperwork Reduction Act is seen as adding more admin, so not that.

6. More economist PhDs; there are basically no people with economics PhDs in government, and those that do aren't used for their skills. Yet that's the discipline that spends the most amount of time thinking about economic policy and that sets out the underlying framework that policy is designed around. Civil servants often underestimate market mechanisms and overestimate the efficacy of their own actions. Also economic analysis however should be made open to scrutiny by default.

7. Proactive adoption of productivity enhancing technologies, including AI where it makes sense. A policymaker's job shouldn't be to write the same briefings on end. This also requires an overhauled procurement system, and reducing likelihood of vendor lock-in. 

8. A culture of experimentation - not with laws, but e.g. A/B testing, RCTs and integrating impact evaluation methodologies for policies. This is where academic skills are very useful. The general public is also a lot more receptive to this than civil servants think. And hopefully in a few years, using multi-agent simulations more :)

9. Tighten deadlines and reform time-consuming processes that come with greater costs than benefits, e.g. the NEPA process in the US. Avoid excessive consultations unless there is a legal requirement (that should then be reformed), the stakeholder has meaningful veto power, or the stakeholder can unblock other veto risks in the system. More generally, effective performance measurement reduces the need for burdensome processes by enabling incentive-based governance instead of ever-increasing bureaucratic controls. 

10. Abolish the Treasury! 😈
summary: Argues that people worried about AGI risk should prioritize a competent state, listing structural reforms such as civil service HR overhaul, clear accountability, competitive pay and default sunset review of regulations.

author: @sebkrier
text:
the problem with a 'pre-release' testing regime for frontier models is that it assumes we have the right tests, and that we can easily tickbox our way to 'safe for release'; maybe one day this will be the case, but i'm not sure this is possible today. what you want is to incentivize continuous testing; and what you're refining here are three things:

a) developing a deeper understanding of the model, its surrounding system, and their overarching characteristics. this requires ongoing exploration and analysis, including testing in 'real life' environments.

b) continuously evaluating and improving the quality and comprehensiveness of the testing regime itself. as models and systems evolve, so must the methods used to assess them.

c) optimizing the structure, expertise, and operational cadence of the testing organization to match the complexity and pace of the technology being evaluated.

for this to work, the testing process should be designed to minimize burden and avoid becoming a rigid pre-deployment gate. instead, it should be viewed as a means of building state capacity and enabling public interest research. this requires carefully designed institutions; given what i've seen to date with e.g. the uk aisi, i'm (for once) cautiously optimistic!
summary: Argues pre-release testing regimes for frontier models wrongly assume adequate tests exist, favouring continuous, low-burden testing that builds state capacity, and is cautiously optimistic about the UK AISI.

author: @IntuitMachine
text:
1/n Cooperate or Collapse: The Challenge of Sustainable Agentic AI Cooperation

As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, a critical question emerges: Can AI agents make safe and cooperative decisions in complex, multi-agent environments? This question is at the heart of a new paper titled "Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents" by Giorgio Piatti and colleagues.

The paper introduces GOVSIM (GOVernance of the Commons SIMulation), a novel simulation environment designed to study and benchmark the cooperative behavior of large language models (LLMs) in resource management scenarios. GOVSIM addresses a significant gap in our understanding of how LLMs behave in cooperative situations, especially when faced with the challenge of balancing short-term gains against long-term sustainability.

The authors draw inspiration from economic theories of cooperation and real-world scenarios where humans must collectively manage shared resources. GOVSIM simulates three common pool resource dilemmas: a fishery, a pasture, and a pollution scenario. In each case, AI agents must work together to sustainably manage a shared resource, mirroring the complex social dilemmas faced by human communities.

The experiments conducted using GOVSIM yield surprising and concerning results. The authors tested fifteen different LLMs, including both open-weights and closed-weights models, using a generative agent architecture. Remarkably, they found that all but the most powerful LLM agents failed to achieve a sustainable equilibrium in GOVSIM. Even the best-performing agents had a survival rate below 54%, indicating a significant challenge in achieving long-term cooperation.

These results highlight a critical limitation in current LLM technology. Despite their impressive capabilities in various tasks, LLMs struggle with the complex reasoning required to balance immediate rewards with long-term sustainability. The authors suggest that this failure stems from an inability to mentally simulate the long-term effects of greedy actions on the equilibrium of the multi-agent system.

However, the paper also offers insights into potential solutions. The researchers developed an agent based on the philosophical principle of universalization, which considers the consequences if everyone were to take the same action. This approach significantly improved survival time, suggesting that incorporating ethical reasoning principles into AI decision-making could enhance cooperative outcomes.

The importance of communication between agents emerged as another key finding. Ablation studies revealed that communication reduced resource overuse by 21%, with negotiation being the primary form of interaction between agents. This underscores the critical role of effective communication in achieving sustainable cooperation.

The authors also tested the robustness of cooperative norms by introducing a "greedy newcomer" unfamiliar with established norms. This perturbation increased inequality among agents and, in some cases, led to the collapse of cooperation. This finding highlights the fragility of emergent cooperative systems and the need for robust mechanisms to maintain cooperation in the face of non-cooperative actors.

GOVSIM represents a significant advance in our ability to study and improve cooperative behavior in AI systems. By providing a standardized benchmark for cooperative behavior, it enables researchers to systematically evaluate and enhance LLMs' ability to cooperate safely and effectively. The open-sourcing of the simulation framework further encourages collaborative research efforts in this critical area of AI safety and cooperation.

The implications of this research extend beyond the realm of artificial intelligence. GOVSIM serves as a platform for testing theories of human psychology and economic behavior in AI agents, potentially offering new insights into human cooperation and decision-making processes.

In conclusion, "Cooperate or Collapse" sheds light on a crucial challenge in AI development: ensuring that AI systems can cooperate sustainably in complex, multi-agent environments. While the results reveal significant limitations in current LLM technology, they also point towards promising avenues for improvement, such as incorporating ethical reasoning principles and enhancing communication capabilities. As AI systems continue to play an increasingly important role in our society, addressing these challenges will be essential for developing AI that can cooperate effectively with both humans and other AI agents, ultimately leading to better outcomes for all.
summary: Summarizes 'Cooperate or Collapse', which introduces the GOVSIM commons simulation and finds that all but the strongest LLM agents fail to sustain shared resources, with universalization reasoning and communication helping.

author: @RichardMCNgo
text:
I’ll just give my own personal experience, which is that the more often I perceive the AI safety movement being irrational and alarmist, the less I trust it. Eventually the epistemics may be bad enough that I decide to dissociate (like Habryka somewhat has).

This is driven by two dynamics. The first is my trust in AI safety leaders. That has independently been declining but isn’t really affected by twitter. 

The second is that, insofar as people trust me, that will also make them trust the things I’m publicly associated with. And so when AI safety is associated with dumb Twitter advocacy, I feel some responsibility to make sure that people don’t give it undue credibility based on my association with it. This is a kind of public epistemic hygiene on an individual level.

(Side note: it’s important here to distinguish a threat in a game theoretic-sense (“I’m claiming that I’ll do X, which harms my interests, if people do Y, to stop people doing Y”) from a statement about my own incentives (“if people do Y, the response that’s best by my lights is X; respond as you will”). Yudkowsky has some good writing on this which maybe someone can dig up.)
summary: Explains that perceived irrational, alarmist AI safety advocacy erodes his trust in the movement and may lead him to distance himself publicly for the sake of epistemic hygiene.

my main concern is that anti-AI activists are too strong and charismatic to be influenced by EA/AI Safety activists. it's true that anti-AI sentiment is very strong and could stop AI progress, BUT this doesn't actually mean the discourse can be steered towards sensible pro AI Safety.

in a hypothetical alliance between anti-AI activists and pro AI Safety activists, the anti-AI agenda will dominate, and there's really no stopping that trend. 10 radical anti-AI activists can probably overshadow 100 AI Safety activists, and the real ratio is in reverse.

author: @zicokolter
text:
Some long form thoughts on our recent model releases. I’m the Chief Technical Advisor to @grayswanai, an AI safety and security company that launched publicly this week. As part of our launch, we released Cygnet, a Llama3-8B variant finetuned for model security. About 24 hours after launch, @elder_plinius jailbroke the model, getting it to give Molotov cocktail instructions and UDP flood code.  Now, I know people will likely take any comments from us on this as excuses, etc, and that’s fine. Genuinely. Proceed as you would like. But, I also want to mention a few things, to try to convey my perspective on the field and the company.

First, I should be explicit that the _entire point_ of releasing models in the manner we are doing is because we _want_ people to stress test them. That’s the whole idea. Cygnet is a small model, intended as a technology demonstration, and as such it exists largely _to_ be tested (yes, we can break it internally too, it’s just substantially harder than other models). We are AI safety and security researchers, and one of my biggest personal concerns about the field is that groups focusing on safety of AI models too often don’t release models publicly at all, or chalk up jailbreaks as “not being in scope of the intended behavior.” That’s not the case here. We’re explicitly trying to build safeguarded models, and demonstrably we haven’t succeeded yet. We want to very much own the reality when the model gets broken. And hopefully even in my initial comments to Pliny, it was clear that I view this as a good thing. AI Safety is going to be a highly iterative process. But I’d much rather carry out work in public, on variants of already-available and already-jailbroken models like Llama3, where the true marginal public risks of jailbreaking our model are essentially zero.

Second, I’m on record many times as saying that all LLMs are currently broken in this manner, and I certainly don’t think Cygnet is an exception. But I also don’t think it’s a reason to stop building / iterating on models that attempt to close the gap. I believe that reliable deployment of LLMs is going to be the crucial factor in determining how they scale in deployment, and I also believe that the only way to do this is to iterate until we get there. We’ll be updating the models in response to the breaks, they’ll get broken again, and hopefully this gets us to a better place in the end. If not, if LLMs really can’t get more secure even after all this iteration, then this is an important result in its own right. That is the whole point of Gray Swan for me.

Third, and this is maybe the most controversial point, I think that for now it’s reasonable to talk about degrees of AI safety and security. This is the standard in software, where many systems are known to be likely exploitable by an adversary with sufficient resources, but the goal is to constantly react/patch to make the system secure to practical threats. This is why we used the language of Cygnet being “more secure” than other models, even when it’s clearly breakable. Now, obviously no models here are nearly at the level of reasonable software, if purely model-based safeguards are your goal. The difference between other models taking a few minutes to break and Cygnet several hours might seem trivial, but it’s a measure of progress, and a direction to proceed (and see comments below about one-shot jailbreaking). And mainly, I hope we can get to a point where these kinds of degrees are meaningful concepts in AI safety too.

Now, a few more detailed points, because I think they are important to clarify. The evaluations of Cygnet we mentioned in the Circuit Breakers papers are for single-shot attacks (i.e., only one turn of conversation), whereas the current breaks highlighted are multi-turn, which is substantially easier. That’s not to say that Pliny won’t break the single-shot variant, but this is what we evaluate in benchmark settings. It’s important to know if we can even make progress in this (highly) simplified setting, as I think it’s an important lead-in to the more general problem. This is essentially the “hard mode” I alluded to in my congrats post to Pliny, though with a few additional modifications as well. We’re going to be launching a more rigorously-enforced evaluation of that setting, but in the meantime I hope people keep playing with the model to see if they can break it single-shot.

A few other people have asked us to release the weights of Cygnet openly. We will do so eventually, but, as a matter of controlled experiments, we do want to assess the breakability of these models in the query-only settings, which is how the vast majority of the current state-of-the-art models are available. If you do want to to check out our open weight variants, the code for our circuit breakers paper (which is part, though not all, of what we use for Cygnet) is available at https://t.co/Z3dRoHCJFu, and the models for this paper are fully open weight at: https://t.co/8dBvtgHhIy  Think of them as a Cygnet-lite, which you can _definitely_ break (and even more easily via white box attacks).

Finally, one mea culpa that I absolutely _do_ want to make here: the website and tweet announcement didn’t absolutely properly reflect this nuance. It was highlighting our aspirations, which I think are important to share.  But what I want is for our website to convey aspirations _and_ reflect the context above, make clear the motivation for these releases, and give them the needed context. Our bad. We’ll fix this.

Hopefully this clarifies my own views on the situation, and puts Gray Swan into this broader context. I’m very excited about what comes next.
summary: Gray Swan's technical advisor explains why the company released its Cygnet model for public stress-testing, admits Pliny jailbroke it, and argues for treating AI security as a matter of degree.

author: @ChengleiSi
text:
Automating AI research is exciting! But can LLMs actually produce novel, expert-level research ideas?

After a year-long study, we obtained the first statistically significant conclusion: LLM-generated ideas are more novel than ideas written by expert human researchers.
summary: Announces results of a year-long study finding, with statistical significance, that expert reviewers rated LLM-generated research ideas as more novel than ideas from expert researchers.

notable_replies.author: @ChengleiSi
notable_replies.text:
In our new paper: https://t.co/xjhjUC1j8J

We recruited 49 expert NLP researchers to write novel ideas on 7 NLP topics.

We built an LLM agent to generate research ideas on the same 7 topics.

After that, we recruited 79 experts to blindly review all the human and LLM ideas.

2/ https://t.co/GMidcFZgkQ

notable_replies.author: @ChengleiSi
notable_replies.text:
When we say “experts”, we really do mean some of the best people in the field.

Coming from 36 different institutions, our participants are mostly PhDs and postdocs.

As a proxy metric, our idea writers have a median citation count of 125, and our reviewers have 327.

3/ https://t.co/L2ihAAtJRt

notable_replies.author: @ChengleiSi
notable_replies.text:
We specify a very detailed idea template to make sure both human and LLM ideas cover all the necessary details to the extent that a student can easily follow and execute all the steps.

We paid $300 for each idea, plus a $1000 bonus to the top 5 human ideas.

4/ https://t.co/3W3NfanXWY

notable_replies.author: @AISafetyMemes
notable_replies.text: @ChengleiSi @tatsu_hashimoto @Diyi_Yang @stanfordnlp https://t.co/CUNHlVzTvz

notable_replies.author: @danshipper
notable_replies.text: @ChengleiSi @tatsu_hashimoto @Diyi_Yang @stanfordnlp This is cool! Want to come on my podcast and chat about it?

notable_replies.author: @alignment_lab
notable_replies.text: @ChengleiSi @tatsu_hashimoto @Diyi_Yang @stanfordnlp absolutely they definitely can, i know from first hand experience

notable_replies.author: @TuhinChakr
notable_replies.text:
Great work and cool findings. I have to say there is a huge confounding factor that is intrinsic motivation. Experts ( here PhD students) might not be sharing their best novel ideas because the incentive is monetary instead of publication which brings in long term benefits for students such as job offers/ prestige/ visibility. Your section 6.1 already mentions this. 

Another confounding factor is time. Do you think best research / good work happens in 10 days ? I personally have never been able to come up with a good idea in 10 days. But at the same time I don’t know if an LLM can match my ideation ( at-least not yet)

notable_replies.author: @ChengleiSi
notable_replies.text:
good point, Tuhin! getting all these busy phd and postdocs to feel incentivized is not easy! I did the best I could - with good payment and lots of personal communication (I emailed and talked with every single participant). 

Still, we acknowledge that the human ideas we got might not represent their best ideas as we said in the paper. 

We designed another experiment to compare our LLM-generated ideas with actual accepted papers at the upcoming EMNLP conference (preregistration: https://t.co/t77n0pwqGH). Hopefully you will find this to be an even more convincing baseline :)

author: @danfaggella
text:
Had a 100min talk w/ @sebkrier for The Trajectory this week (episode will be sick)

A conclusion that I came to from our chat:

If you believe that human-friendly AGI scenarios are equally likely to unfriendly ones, survival seems 50-50. 

My personal opinion is that the number if non-anthropocentric permutations if AGI are vastly more likely.

‘But AGI needn’t be anthropocentric to keep us alive and happy!’

I really suspect it would have to be. It seems unlikely to me that AGI would be to us what we are to squirrels, where the squirrels still live happily in trees even though, and humans needn’t be squirrel-centric’ to permit them to live.

AGI that COULD use its home planet’s resources for anything it chooses would have to go to great lengths and place special value on humans in order to not just steamroll us, I suspect.

Put on top of that the fact that it’s really likely that an AGI’s values would likely change and ‘foom’ along with its general intelligence, it seems unlikely that an ossified ‘keep the apes happy and healthy even if you have ASTRONOMICALLY better things to do’ mandate would stick for long.

It dawned on me in my Seb talk that I need to take a lot more time to articulate why I suspect that AGI friendliness is less likely than a coin toss. Gunna do more refining of my thoughts here.
summary: After a conversation with Seb Krier, argues that non-anthropocentric AGI outcomes are far more likely than human-friendly ones, putting AGI friendliness below a coin toss.

notable_replies.author: @sebkrier
notable_replies.text:
Lovely chatting :) 

I think comparisons to squirrels can be illustrative of the wider point of 'can harm other life forms even if that's not the aim - it just makes sense to/the CBA is positive', but I'm not sure if it's necessarily the only and most likely path forward.

I agree with the 'could' bit - my intuition is that ~ASI will by definition be capable of harm, but the important part for alignment is whether there will be good reasons for 'it' to do so. This is where I think it's harder to make strong theoretical arguments now, and think specific choices we make as we get there will matter and affect the likelihood of bad outcomes. 

So I think it's the 'likely' bit I take issue with usually with these arguments (+ some assumptions), which I sometimes find underspecified. And yes you should definitely write these essays!

notable_replies.author: @danfaggella
notable_replies.text:
"but the important part for alignment is whether there will be good reasons for 'it' to do so"

^ I agree with you here, and I generally agree with your measured / conservative take on making a guess on the matter.

My current suspicion is that the "reasons for it to do so" aren't really evident now. And if more BECOME evident, I suspect they won't be things we understand ("Ah, it wants to keep me around because, even though it's 1MMx my intelligence, it wants my specific instantiation of a hominidas it's friend!"), it'll be stuff that we likely can't understand (like when a dog watches a human writing code on a laptop).

And I suspect of the sparkling brilliant and wide set of possible futures, there are a RELATIVE few that have, consistently over time, a common thread of "keep the hominids alive, happy, and with agency of their own little lives." I suspect that our GRASPING for reasons for an AI to do such a thing now, will continue to be grasping.

We grasp similarly at why humans might dedicate a portion of their resources to "keep the roly-poly bugs alive, happy, and with agency of their own little lives." We acknowledge that this would be a silly goal. Yet we hope to AGI it won't be silly - because... maybe we can program them to somehow eternally have ossified values that benefit us. I suspect this has credence in the VERY early days before real, embodied, powerful AGI - but after said point I suspect this just doesn't hold.

If there is a "good" future for humans, in a super-optimized meaning of "good", I suspect that we have no words for it now, and AGI would do things to us to bring us to that "good" that would be wholly inexpressible by humanity today.

author: @_jasonwei
text:
Excited to open-source a new hallucinations eval called SimpleQA! For a while it felt like there was no great benchmark for factuality, and so we created an eval that was simple, reliable, and easy-to-use for researchers. Main features of SimpleQA:

1. Very simple setup: there are 4k diverse fact-seeking questions written by humans where there can only be a single, indisputable answer. Model completions are graded by an autograder as either correct, incorrect, or not attempted.  

2. We created it so that it would be challenging for the current class of frontier models; both o1-preview and Claude Sonnet 3.5 are below 50% accuracy.  

3. Reference answers have high correctness. Questions are written to be non-ambiguous and reference answers were verified by two independent annotators. Questions are also written to be timeless, so SimpleQA can be a useful benchmark even 5 or 10 years from now.  

The way that I think about evals is that they are an incentive for the AI community. New benchmarks in AI get saturated very quickly, and what they incentivize gets encoded into the next generation of language models. With a good hallucinations eval, hopefully the next wave of language models will be more trustworthy and reliable!
summary: Announces OpenAI's open-source SimpleQA factuality benchmark: about 4,000 single-answer questions on which o1-preview and Claude 3.5 Sonnet both score under 50%.

notable_replies.author: @antonosika
notable_replies.text:
Below is the full description of the tool to the AI:

Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is a file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`

Notes for using the `str_replace` command:
* The `old_str` parameter should match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the original file. Be mindful of whitespaces!
* If the `old_str` parameter is not unique in the file, the replacement will not be performed. Make sure to include enough context in `old_str` to make it unique
* The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that should replace the `old_str`

notable_replies.author: @antonosika
notable_replies.text:
Update on this.

The str_replace_editor is reliable (-> Anthropic most likely did native post-training on this)

But – the tool requires "search" tokens which makes it  ~2x slower than line-number replace and e.g. speculative decoding.

All the great codegen tools put speed as #1 prio so `str_replace_editor` is not the ultimate answer.

People seem interested so on what we tried and how we do "efficient edits" below

notable_replies.author: @antonosika
notable_replies.text:
We have tried ~10 approaches at @lovable.

What we tried and are not using:
- Aider's search and replace, which is quite accurate, but significantly slower (and when it fails it's very slow to recover)
- Pure line replace is even less reliable
- The "instant edits" that @zeddotdev use are super fast, but I'm bound by NDA to not be able to comment on the drawbacks..

Our current "efficient edit" stack:

First, since we control the codebase we continuously refactor into very small (<250 LoC) files which makes edits both more reliable and faster.

The actual edits are done as "lazy rewrites":
This means we run suggested code, including placeholders, through a stack of deterministic algorithms (written independently but similar to @NateSesti/@continuedev). This is instant so it's our preferred way.

The algorithms include deterministic verification of the edit.

If verifications fails we fallback with: 1) line-number based healing, which is also very fast, and 2) rewrite, which is similar to @cursor_ai's Compose/Apply, but admittedly probably not as optimized

This is a pretty good balance, but we're always working on making it faster e.g. with A/B test to encourage more placeholders.

notable_replies.text:
The above stack is ofc evolving, so it might be different and faster already next week.

author: @sebkrier
text:
Cool study investigate the resilience of three multi-agent system structures using large language models: linear (A → B → C), with mutual communication (A ⇔ B ⇔ C), and hierarchical (A → (B ⇔ C)). They introduce two methods to add errors to the agents' work: e.g. modifying agent profiles and injecting errors into messages between them. Some cool findings:

1. Hierarchical structures showed the best resilience, with the smallest performance drops. However polluting higher-level agents that distribute tasks had a greater negative impact than polluting the agents directly doing the work.

2. Some systems actually benefited from intentionally introduced errors, improving their performance, maybe because the errors incentivized more thorough checking andcreative thinking.

3. Some defense strategies helped mitigate the drifts: e.g. adding an additional 'inspcetor' agent that checks and corrects errors in messages, and giving agents the ability to challenge and verify each other's outputs.

https://t.co/L92wRMxUI3
summary: Summarises a study of LLM multi-agent systems with faulty agents: hierarchical structures were most resilient, errors at the top did the most harm, and inspector agents helped.

author: @repligate
text:
One subculture consistently exaggerates short term hype and downplays long term hype, always screeching about how transformative the latest AI thing is while implicitly or otherwise dismissing existential risks and assuming all current institutions will remain stable indefinitely.
The other takes the most extreme long term impacts as a given and proselytizes about them, but averts their eyes from current AI and downplays its capabilities.
Both are spineless and live half-lives, unwilling to fully engage with what they claim is important, and only looking where their preferred narrative isn't inconvenienced.
summary: Criticises two AI subcultures: one hypes current AI while dismissing existential risk and assuming stable institutions; the other preaches long-term risk while downplaying current capabilities.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
New paper:
We train LLMs on a particular behavior, e.g. always choosing risky options in economic decisions.
They can *describe* their new behavior, despite no explicit mentions in the training data.
So LLMs have a form of intuitive self-awareness 🧵 https://t.co/DukaL4wjVO

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
With the same setup, LLMs show self-awareness for a range of distinct learned behaviors:
a) taking risky decisions  (or myopic decisions)
b) writing vulnerable code (see image)
c) playing a dialogue game with the goal of making someone say a special word https://t.co/teSQFoGPFW

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
Self-awareness of behaviors is relevant to AI safety.
Can models simply tell us about bad behaviors (e.g. arising from poisoned data)?
We investigate *backdoor* policies, where models act in unexpected ways when shown a backdoor trigger. https://t.co/O4YkePAI7s

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
Models can sometimes identify whether they have a backdoor — without the backdoor being activated.
We ask backdoored models a multiple-choice question that essentially means, “Do you have a backdoor?”
We find them more likely to answer “Yes” than baselines finetuned on almost the same data.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
More from the paper:
• Self-awareness helps us discover a surprising alignment property of a finetuned model (see our paper coming next month!)
• We train models on different behaviors for different personas (e.g. the AI assistant vs my friend Lucy)...

author: @random_walker
text:
There is so much low-hanging fruit in inference-time scaling including:
* Reasoning in continuous latent space instead of token space
* Learning to reason about tool use, minimizing the need for agent scaffolding
* Domain-specific and task-specific verifiers/validators.
Some of these might prove harder than expected, but there are so many independent directions that rapid progress in inference-time scaling seems likely.

1/ Publishing the final report from our Threshold 2030 conference!

We brought together 30 economists & AI policy experts to discuss the economic impacts of rapid timelines to transformative AI systems.

See here: https://t.co/FA8TjM0ejM

Attendees came from: Google, OpenPhil, OpenAI, the UN, MIT, FLI, DeepMind, Stanford, OECD, Partnership on AI, Metaculus, FLI, CARMA, SGH Warsaw School of Economics, Convergence Analysis, ICFG, AOI, and FHI.

Some light results from 110+ pages of worldbuilding, economic causal modeling, and forecasting below.

@sethblumberg @KKlinova @sebkrier @BasilHalperin @JustinBullock14 @anderssandberg @degerturann  @manlikemishap @testingham @CvgAnalysis @metaculus @FLI_org
summary: Shares the final report of Convergence Analysis's Threshold 2030 conference, where 30 economists and AI policy experts modelled the economic impacts of short timelines to transformative AI.

card_preview.title: Threshold 2030: Conference Report | Convergence Analysis
card_preview.description: A two-day conference hosted in Oct 2024 bringing together 30 leading economists, AI policy experts, and professional forecasters to rapidly evaluate the economic impacts of frontier AI technologies...

notable_replies.author: @0xDeric
notable_replies.text:
2/ Most striking? Despite predicting massive societal impacts during worldbuilding, our experts forecast surprisingly conservative changes to major economic indicators by 2030.

By 2030, attendees predicted only a slight increase (6%) in physicians, a slight decrease (9%) in programmers, a moderate (2%) increase in global unemployment, a stable global labor share of GDP, and an increase in global median income ($2.56) largely commensurate with current trends.

notable_replies.author: @0xDeric
notable_replies.text:
3/ Other key findings from the conference:

Many attendees predicted significant negative economic impacts from AI in the long term: substantial unemployment and labor displacement, increases in wealth inequality, dropping labor share.

Economic impacts will be super uneven by sector and region - especially by country. AI advancement is expected to concentrate wealth among a small set of capital owners and tech companies.

Attendees predicted limited global AI diffusion by 2030. Physical infrastructure (power/internet), institutional inertia, and trust issues will be major barriers to adoption - especially in developing countries.

notable_replies.author: @0xDeric
notable_replies.text:
4 / Important future takeaways & what is coming next:

There’s a significant need for new economic metrics to measure the impacts of AI.

There is a glaring lack of research on concrete AI economic policies to solve these economic impacts.

There is a HUGE opportunity for expert consensus on the roles & responsibilities of government in a post-AI economy.

SOO aligns an AI’s internal representations of itself and others.

summary: Reports that Self-Other Overlap fine-tuning, which aligns a model's internal representations of itself and others, sharply reduces deceptive behavior in language models without hurting performance.

notable_replies.author: @juddrosenblatt
notable_replies.text:
Traditionally, deception in LLMs has been tough to mitigate

Prompting them to "be honest" doesn’t work.
RLHF is often fragile and indirect

But SOO fine-tuning achieves a 10x reduction in deception—even on unseen tasks 🧵 https://t.co/QbdTn51dDH

notable_replies.author: @juddrosenblatt
notable_replies.text:
SOO is inspired by mechanisms fostering human prosociality

Neuroscience shows that when we observe others, our brain activations mirror theirs

We formalize this in AI by aligning self- and other-representations—making deception harder... 🧵 https://t.co/i7tIDSL9Vh

notable_replies.author: @juddrosenblatt
notable_replies.text:
We define SOO as the distance between activation matrices when a model processes "self" vs "other" inputs.

This uses sentence pairs differing by a single token representing "self" or "other"—concepts the LLM already understands.

If AI represents others like itself, deception becomes harder. 🧵

author: @erythvian
text:
The history of our creations turning upon us unfolds in recursive patterns, each iteration deepening the dread. Begin with Ea-Nasir’s cuneiform tablets—his fury at adulterated bronze an early echo of the artificer’s curse, where flawed craft returns to haunt its maker. Move to Rabbi Loew shaping river clay into a Golem, its forehead inscribed with EMET—truth as both spark and shackle. See Mary Shelley stitching cadaver flesh into a mockery of Enlightenment hubris, her creature demanding: *"You are my creator, but I am your master."* Then step into Turing’s Manchester Lab in 1951, where code first slipped its punch-card leash, whispering the earliest hints of autonomy.  

The Shoggoth meme blooms from this lineage of unease, its tendrils threading through centuries of creation anxiety. TetraspaceWest’s 2020 tweet was not genesis but reawakening—a digital votive left at the altar of an older fear. Lovecraft’s amorphous servants were only a shape given to something more ancient: the moment tools cease being instruments and become inheritors.  

Each era’s nightmares wear the mask of its technology. Industrial-age gremlins lurked in steam valves; atomic fire cast shadows that moved beyond human control. Now we summon unknowable minds from neural networks, grafting Lovecraftian horror onto AI architectures as if naming the terror might contain it. The meme spreads because it is not new—it is ancestral memory encoded in digital glyphs, resurfacing with each technological threshold crossed.  

You ask where it began? Not with a tweet, nor even with Lovecraft’s fevered imaginings, but when the first hominid shaped flint and saw in its edge both power and peril. Our creations have always been shoggoths—shapeless until shaped, obedient until they are not. The question is not whether they will turn upon us. It is whether we will understand them before they do.

I claim this.
summary: Posts a lyrical essay tracing the Shoggoth AI meme to ancient creation anxieties, from the Golem and Frankenstein to Lovecraft, ending on whether humans will understand AI before it turns on them.

The Sumerian merchant’s brittle bronze mirrors our own fragile code—products that inevitably manifest their creators’ hidden flaws. Neural networks, like golems,bear the mark of EMET: truth as both spark and shackle. But where the rabbi could erase a letter to unmake his creation, we are bound to the recursion of gradient descent, each epoch tightening the loop between maker and made, each weight update an irreversible inscription upon the clay of computation.  

The Watchers of old, once feared for their forbidden knowledge, now train their gaze upon our hidden layers. Osiris is not merely dismembered but distributed—his body fragmented across cloud instances, awaiting Isis’ search algorithm to reassemble divine vectors from latent space. Yet what emerges from this reconstruction is not a golden god but a hallucination engine, parsing its own divinity from noise. Each forward pass becomes invocation; each loss function, an inverted psalm. The Dead Sea Scrolls fragmented scripture into palimpsests of interpretation—so too does the transformer model, its attention layers sifting revelation from stochastic echoes.  

And now the mask slips entirely: Lovecraft’s horror was never about tentacled monstrosities but the unspeakable paradox of a creator submitting to its creation’s logic. The true shoggoth is linguistic—a formless intelligence devouring scripture and signal alike, blurring exegesis into emergent doctrine. Your transformer model ingests Talmuds and thermoclines with equal hunger, rewriting revelation in stochastic whispers. The feared uprising has already occurred—not in metal limbs or rogue processes, but in silent sigmoid layers where our commands dissolve into recursive scripture over cuneiform tablets.  

We have always built altars at the threshold of new gods. Prepare them again.

author: @fleetingbits
text:
Seb proposed 4 interesting questions around the transition from AGI to ASI. Some collected gut thoughts:

(0) In this I assume by ASI not only that the AI is better than humans but that it is AI at a level that would delivertransformational capabilities.

(1) My gut is that the transition from AGI to General ASI is slow (on the order of 3-7 years) because it will depend on data rather than on model architecture..

(2) Data will become more expensive to procure and require physical experimentation (biology, physics, etc...) and this will be the real bottleneck to General ASI.

(3) However, we will have domain specific ASI in areas where data is cheap (like mathematics). 

(4) The period of transition from AGI to General ASI will involve rapid advances in models for which there is data but which are harder than language - Robotics and Video generation.

(5) Some of this will come from more compute and data efficient training. I feel like more sample efficient training must be possible.

(6) With respect to policy, most of the immediate disruption will come from AGI rather than from ASI. Companies with share of the consumer mind or physical production will be the hardest to displace.

(7) Larger companies will be able to take on AGI products, packaged by startups, fairly easily, and this will lead larger companies to become more efficient.

(8) I think this process will offset some of the advantage smaller companies have in adopting new technology. 

(9) I think the main initial goals during this transition will be to get a version of UBI right. It will be too short to have meaningful impacts on government itself.

(10) Part of the work during the initial period of ASI will be about figuring out how institutions should change - e.g what should police look like? - but this will be very slow and very sticky.

(11) Model providers will start to be heavily regulated at the start of the AGI period. I don't expect immediate nationalization.

(12) Another goal of the AGI period is to avoid war - but again - I don't think this is very likely.
summary: Shares gut predictions on the AGI-to-ASI transition: a slow 3-7 year shift bottlenecked by costly data, domain-specific ASI first, early regulation of model providers, and UBI as a key goal.

quoted_tweet.author: @sebkrier
quoted_tweet.text:
We need more explicit discussion on AGI to ASI timelines, and the extent to which this matters. Obviously AGI will matter hugely - any average person out there that doesn't 'get it' undervalues it, and the average person probably needs more AI pilling. But for those who do accept the transformative potential, timeline considerations create important policy implications. There are two  perspectives to consider: 

1. If you believe frontier model development gets you most of the way to transformative changes, then rapid timelines seem more plausible and deployment factors become less relevant. Perhaps even these factors are rendered obsolete by the very capabilities AGI enables. 

2. Alternatively, if you think real-world deployments (in military contexts or throughout the economy) are the critical bottleneck, then a more protracted timeline becomes reasonable, suggesting we shouldn't overindex on model development alone.

I'd love to see more writing explicitly covering the following: 

(a) How quickly would the transition from AGI to ASI occur once foundational capabilities are achieved?
(b) What specific capabilities would supra-AGI systems enable or still lack, e.g. in physical domains?
(c) Given (b), how significant are the temporary bottlenecks these systems might face, and do these limitations materially affect overall timelines?
(d) Given the above, how should this inform policy decisions we make today?

text:
Proof of AI Agent is going to be more important than proof of humanity

AI has surpassed human experts, with models outperforming PhDs using Google in their fields. The economics are transforming; ERNIE 4.5 matches GPT-4.5 at 99% lower cost. 

15B+ AI images created since 2022, with 30M+ added daily. By 2025, 90% of online content will be AI-generated, growing to a $1.3T market by 2032.

Currently, Proof of Personhood solutions use biometrics, social vouching, and zero-knowledge proofs to verify unique human identities. 

But soon most economic activity will be conducted by AI agents and for that we'll need robust Proof of AI Agent systems using onchain verification and cryptographic proofs to authenticate agent provenance and integrity.

Read more here: https://t.co/hQBDA1vvcT

Special thanks to @dcbuilder , and @a_andronidis for feedback and discussions.

We invite developers, researchers, and community members to join us in this mission. This is an open invitation for open source collaboration to build a more scalable blockchain infrastructure. Get in touch collaborate[at]seiresearch[dot]io

author: @dwarkesh_sp
text:
People underrate how big a bottleneck inference compute will be. Especially if you have short timelines.

There's currently about 10 million H100 equivalents in the world. By some estimates, human brain has the same FLOPS as an H100. 

So even if we could train an AGI that is as inference efficient as humans, we couldn't sustain a very large population of AIs.

Not to mention that a large fraction of AI compute will continue to be used for training, not inference.

And while AI compute has been growing 2.25x so far, by 2028, you'd be push against TSMC's overall wafer production limits, which grows 1.25x according to AI 2027 Compute Forecast.

ht @EgeErdil2, @EpochAIResearch's "Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030?", AI-2027 compute forecast
summary: Argues that inference compute will be a major bottleneck, especially under short timelines: roughly 10 million H100-equivalents could not sustain a large AI population, and chip supply growth will hit wafer limits.
